title: Emergence of Resonating Valence-Bond Correlations in Stretched Graphene
authors: Sam Azadi, A. Principi, T. D. Kühne, M. S. Bahramy
abstract: Electronic correlations in graphene are generally considered weak due to the large bandwidth of its $π$ electrons. Here we show that tensile expansion of the honeycomb lattice provides a direct route to enhancing correlation effects. Using variational and diffusion quantum Monte Carlo, we compare a conventional Jastrow-Slater determinant wave function with a resonating-valence-bond (RVB) Jastrow-antisymmetrized geminal product ansatz for a series of stretched graphene lattices. We find that the energy gain of the RVB state relative to the single-determinant description increases with bond expansion up to a critical strain $δ_{\mathrm{cr}}$, and decreases beyond it, revealing a nonmonotonic evolution of electronic correlations. The crossover is found to occur in the range $15\% < δ_{\mathrm{cr}} < 20\%$, in agreement with mechanical stability limits. This behavior indicates a transition from a weakly correlated Dirac semimetal to a regime with enhanced non-dynamic correlation and short-range singlet pairing. Our results provide direct many-body evidence that lattice expansion drives graphene into a regime where RVB-like correlations become energetically favorable, offering a simple route to tuning correlation effects in Dirac materials.
summary: The research uses advanced Quantum Monte Carlo methods to study how tensile strain affects electron correlations in graphene. By comparing standard and Resonating Valence Bond (RVB) wave functions, the authors find that stretching the lattice enhances correlation effects up to a critical strain ($\delta_{cr}$). This demonstrates a tunable pathway to stabilize highly correlated electronic states in Dirac materials.
main_problem: To determine how tensile strain modifies electronic correlations in graphene, potentially driving a transition into a regime dominated by Resonating Valence Bond (RVB) physics.
main_result: Tensile expansion enhances RVB-like singlet correlations up to a critical strain ($\delta_{cr} \approx 15\% - 20\%$), where the energy gain of the RVB ansatz peaks, indicating a nonmonotonic evolution of correlation strength.
method: Variational and Diffusion Quantum Monte Carlo (VMC/DMC) simulations are used to calculate ground state energies by comparing two wave function ansätze: a standard Jastrow-Slater determinant and an RVB-based Geminal Product ansatz.
model_or_system: The system is graphene, modeled on its honeycomb lattice. The study investigates the effect of biaxial tensile strain ($\delta$) on the electronic correlation energy, treating electron interactions beyond simple mean-field approximations.
key_observables: Energy gain ($\Delta E = E_{	ext{RVB}} - E_{	ext{JSD}}$) as a function of strain $\delta$; band structure renormalization (pDOS); total ground state energy.
important_parameters: Tensile strain ($\delta$); Critical Strain ($\delta_{cr}$) in the $15\% < \delta_{cr} < 20\%$ range; System sizes ($N=16, 36, 64$).
main_assumptions: The use of fixed-node approximation in DMC; The necessity of using an RVB ansatz (JAGP) to capture static correlation effects neglected by single-determinant forms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy gain ($\Delta E$) vs. strain, showing nonmonotonic behavior with a peak/crossover point at $\delta_{cr}$. Tables present calculated total energies using both JSD and JAGP wave functions across various strains.
paper_structure: The paper systematically calculates ground state properties (energy) for graphene under increasing biaxial strain ($\delta$) by comparing the results from two increasingly sophisticated quantum many-body wave function ansätze (JSD vs. RVB/AGP), revealing a critical transition point.
why_interesting: This work provides direct, quantitative evidence that external mechanical tuning (strain) can be used as a simple knob to tune fundamental electronic interactions in Dirac materials, potentially stabilizing exotic correlated phases like those described by RVB theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Energy difference ∆E = EJAGP −EJSD as a func- tion of in-plane biaxial strain δ, obtained from VMC and DMC calculations for system sizes N = 16, 36, and 64 atoms. The shaded region indicates the critical strain δcr, where ∆E reaches its minimum; for δ > δcr, ∆E increases with further stretching. The nonmonotonic behavior reflects the enhance- ment of static, RVB-like singlet correlations up to δcr, followed by a crossover to a different correlation regime at larger strain.

FIG. 2. DFT band structure of graphene obtained at biaxial stretch δ = 5%, 10%, 15%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%. The shaded regions in the conduction bands along the M–Γ and K–Γ directions highlight the crossings between the π∗and σ∗bands. The evolution of these crossings with increasing δ is shown. The arrow at the M point indicates the gap between the two lowest conduction bands, which decreases with increasing δ due to the reduced slope and flattening of the π∗band.
